paper.title: Research Ethics Committees as an intervention point to promote a priori sample size calculations

claims.text: 19 of the 20 sampled REC template forms requested the planned sample size.
12 of the 20 forms requested a justification of the sample size.
6 of the 20 forms requested a sample size calculation.
Results were generally similar between US and UK universities: almost all requested the sample size, 60% requested a justification, and 20% (UK) to 40% (US) requested a sample size calculation.
We sampled 19 US universities and 14 UK universities to gain access to template ethics submission forms from 10 universities in each country.
The NIH drug/device and behavioural/social forms requested sample size, justification and a calculation; the NHS HRA form requested all three with the calculation 'if applicable'.
Six of the 7 RECs that declined to share their ethics form stated they could not because they use an online submission system.
The forms were independently double-coded; all coding matched except 1 instance regarding sample size calculation, and in 4 cases the second coder chose 'indirectly requested'.
'Indirectly requested a sample size calculation' means the form prefaced the request with 'if applicable' (n=2) or asked for 'statistical planning including sample size justification' (n=1).
The study is descriptive with no inferential statistics and no sample size calculation of its own.

findings.location: Abstract p.1 and Discussion p.5 ('19 of 20', '12 of 20', '6 of 20') vs Results p.4 and Figure 1
findings.evidence: The denominators differ between the Abstract/Discussion and the Results. The Abstract and Discussion state the three outcomes over 20 forms ('19 of them', '12 of 20', '6 of 20'). The Results state them as percentages of the 10 included forms per country ('60%', '20% (UK) to 40% (US)'), and the authors' stored Table 1 counts only the 10 US + 10 UK university forms (sample size 9 + 10 = 19; justification 6 + 6 = 12; calculation explicit 2 + 1 = 3 plus indirect 2 + 1 = 3, total 6). The data file also contains 3 national-level rows (NIH phase 2/3, NIH behavioural, NHS HRA) that are excluded from Table 1 by the `!is.na(expenditure_rank)` filter in code/analysis.Rmd. The paper never states that the national bodies are excluded from the 20, so a reader cannot tell whether '20 forms' means 20 university forms or 20 forms including the national bodies (which would be 23 coded forms).
findings.question_for_authors: Do the '20 forms' in the Abstract and Discussion refer only to the 20 university forms (excluding the NIH and NHS HRA forms), and could the exclusion of the national bodies be stated explicitly?

findings.location: Abstract p.1 ('6 requested a sample size calculation') vs Figure 1 caption p.5 and stored Table 1
findings.evidence: The 6 is a sum of two coding categories: explicit calculation (US 2 + UK 1 = 3) and indirect calculation (US 2 + UK 1 = 3), 3 + 3 = 6. The Abstract does not say that half of the 6 were coded only as indirect ('if applicable' n=2, 'statistical planning including sample size justification' n=1). A reader of the Abstract alone would take 6 as forms that ask for a calculation outright; the explicit-only count is 3 of 20.
findings.question_for_authors: Should the Abstract report the explicit (3 of 20) and indirect (3 of 20) counts separately?

findings.location: Figure 1 caption p.4-5 ('Six of the 7 RECs that declined to share their ethics form, stated they could not share it because they use an online submission system') vs data/rec_data_raw.csv
findings.evidence: The data file codes 7 declining rows: form_available = 'declined' (1, Harvard University) and 'declined_online' (6: Wisconsin-Madison, Cornell, UNC Chapel Hill, Manchester, King's College London, Bristol). The codebook defines 'declined' as a REC representative responding that they will not share a private ethics form, and 'declined_online' as responding that they cannot share it because it is an online submission portal. The caption's 6 of 7 is consistent with the data, but the paper does not report which single REC declined for another reason, and the caption's wording ('stated they could not share it because they use an online submission system') is the only place this reason is documented.
findings.question_for_authors: Which REC declined for a reason other than an online submission system, and what was the reason?

findings.evidence: Claim 'Most REC template forms request the planned sample size, while only a minority request a sample size calculation' holds in 21 of 24 universes (88%). The 3 universes where it fails are all US-only: (a) US + all_forms + obtained denominator + indirect counted (6 of 12 forms request a calculation = 50%, not a minority); (b) US + universities + sampled denominator + indirect excluded (sample-size share 9/19 = 47%, below half); (c) US + universities + sampled denominator + indirect counted (9/19 = 47%). Pooled US+UK the claim holds in 8 of 8 universes; UK-only in 8 of 8. The US-only '40% requested a calculation' statement is the fragile part: it is 4/10 with the paper's denominator and 6/12 if the two NIH forms are added.
findings.question_for_authors: Should the US calculation share be reported with the national bodies included (6 of 12) and with a confidence interval, given that it is the only country-level result that changes with defensible choices?

findings.evidence: 2 data-exclusion step(s): filter@31, filter@32. Candidate forks for the multiverse stage.

findings.evidence: Claim C8 cannot be re-computed: no available data or code behind its evidence.
Claim C10 cannot be re-computed: no available data or code behind its evidence.

The paper reports that two team members coded the forms independently and that all coding matched except 1 instance, with 4 further cases where the second coder chose 'indirectly requested'. The capsule contains only one coded column per outcome (sample_size, justification, calculation) and no per-coder file, so the disagreement count and the direction of the 4 recodes cannot be checked from the materials.
findings.question_for_authors: Could the two coders' separate coding sheets be deposited so the disagreement count can be verified?

findings.evidence: The Methods say US universities were sampled by NCSES R&D expenditure (Table 20, '2020' column) and UK universities by HESA 'Total expenditure'. The data file's expenditure_rank column skips ranks 19 (US) and 9 (UK) and contains 3 rows with no rank (the national bodies), so the ranks are not a contiguous top-10-per-country list; the paper does not explain the skipped ranks or how ties were handled. The sampling frame itself (NCSES/HESA tables) is not deposited, so the ranking cannot be re-derived.
findings.question_for_authors: Why are expenditure ranks 19 (US) and 9 (UK) absent from the sampled list, and could the NCSES/HESA extracts used for ranking be deposited?

findings.evidence: The paper does not report inter-rater agreement statistics (e.g. Cohen's kappa) for the three coded outcomes, only a raw disagreement count (1 instance). With 20 forms and near-ceiling prevalence for sample size (19/20), kappa would be unstable, but the absence of any agreement statistic limits how far the coding reliability can be judged.
findings.question_for_authors: Could an agreement statistic (or the full 2x2 coding table per outcome) be reported?

findings.location: Results p.4 ('Results were generally similar between US and UK universities')
findings.evidence: The US-UK comparison rests on 10 forms per country. The paper reports no uncertainty for the country-specific percentages (20% UK vs 40% US for calculation), and with n=10 per country a difference of 2 of 10 forms is within sampling noise; the paper explicitly says it performs no inferential statistics, so the 'generally similar' statement is a description, not a tested comparison.
findings.question_for_authors: Would the authors add exact confidence intervals (e.g. Clopper-Pearson) for the country-specific proportions so readers can judge the US-UK difference?

findings.evidence: 3 multiply-reported quantities agree across locations; 33 re-computed values match the paper.
